speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: asked the Prime Minister whether the Government will commit to setting up a Commission of Inquiry to review its response to COVID-19 and, if so, when will this inquiry take place.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean) (for the Prime Minister)
text: It was an unprecedented crisis that extended beyond public health and threatened both lives and livelihoods.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Countries, especially those which encountered the virus relatively early such as Singapore, had to quickly adapt our contingency plans in the midst of doing battle, to deal with the particularly severe challenges posed by this virus.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Every Singaporean has had a part to play.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Our response has by no means been perfect.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean) (for the Prime Minister)
text: We adapted and improved along the way, sharing experiences with other countries as we collectively gained more knowledge of the virus and how to deal with it.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean) (for the Prime Minister)
text: We must thoroughly analyse and learn from our experience, the entire crisis, in all its aspects, from start to finish, just as we did from SARS 17 years ago which helped us greatly in our response this time.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The aim is to understand what we have done well and what we have not, so that we can do better the next time.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean) (for the Prime Minister)
text: However, right now, our agencies remain in the thick of battle.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Their resources are totally committed; they are stretched dealing with the pandemic, which is far from over.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Even as we fight the current battle, we are constantly evaluating, learning, innovating and building new capabilities and capacities to stay ahead of this fast-moving virus.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean) (for the Prime Minister)
text: As a result, we are in a much safer position now than last year.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean) (for the Prime Minister)
text: But COVID-19 will not disappear soon and with new variants continuing to emerge, there could yet be new twists and turns, some perhaps for the worse, but others hopefully for the better.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean) (for the Prime Minister)
text: We have made preparations for a long battle.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean) (for the Prime Minister)
text: But with the unprecedented speed at which effective vaccines have been developed and the pace of our vaccination programme, we can see the light at the end of the tunnel.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean) (for the Prime Minister)
text: When we have the vast majority of our population fully vaccinated, we should be able to live with the virus endemic in our population and gradually shift into a new normal, along with most of the countries in the rest of the world.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean) (for the Prime Minister)
text: There will be lessons to learn from that shift too.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean) (for the Prime Minister)
text: But we are not in a new normal yet.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Meanwhile, we are learning and adapting as we fight the virus, whether it is COVID-19 testing, contact tracing, management of dormitories, isolation procedures for foreign arrivals, or safe management measures.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The purpose of the AAR is for us to learn valuable lessons to improve our response for future pandemics.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean) (for the Prime Minister)
text: We want participants in the AAR to be open and forthcoming, to be reflective and thoughtful and be candid on their experiences and decisions, to acknowledge shortcomings and where we could and should have done better, even as they analyse successes.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The structure of the AAR must fit this purpose.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I also note that there are other countries, the United Kingdom, for example, and the state Legislature of Victoria which has already actually delivered a report on the government's handling of the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I understood the Senior Minister when he said that there will be input from the public, but what sort of shape and form is the Government considering if it is not going to be a Commission of Inquiry?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Senior Minister said that there is a quasi-judicial aspect to Commissions of Inquiry.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But Commissions of Inquiry also involve matters of public policy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Multi-agency issues of grave public concern have also found themselves to be subject of a Commission of Inquiry as opposed to an AAR.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, just to reiterate the question: what sort of review and how can the public play a part in the review that the Government has in mind?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But we certainly want to learn all the lessons that we have, including those which can be submitted by members of the public who have views and informed views particularly.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In my career in the Public Service, I have been the subject of, the convenor of, and participated in many inquiries of various kinds.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: It must suit the purpose for which we set up these inquiries or reviews for.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In my experience, a Commission of Inquiry (COI) is probably best suited to look into a singular event that has occurred in a specific moment or instant in time, such as a building collapse and a major accident.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But I do not think the pandemic fits well into such a situation.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In fact, many lessons have already been learnt along the way, not necessarily though formal AARs or a COI, but because of actual ground experience in which the agencies have adapted and adjusted their response, both in order to be more effective but also in response to an evolving virus and evolving situations.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Like the original answer to the PQ, I take the Senior Minister's point.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I am not sure whether the AAR that the Senior Minister has in mind will be as broad-ranging as a Commission of Inquiry could potentially be but we await information from the Government in this regard.
